title: Nickel Mines (2006)
hook: an Amish community forgave and embraced the family of the gunman who killed their children

segments.voice: Yesterday, Gelassenheit: yieldedness, letting go of self-will. Your line was let go. Which small argument did you let the other person win? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

Nickel Mines is a small village in Lancaster County, Pennsylvania, in Amish farm country. One morning a man walked into its one-room Amish schoolhouse and shot the girls there. Some of them died, and so did he, by his own hand. There's no need to say more about that morning. What made people far away stop and look came after. Soon after, Amish neighbors went to the gunman's family. They came to say they forgave him, and to comfort his widow and children, who were grieving too. When he was buried, Amish mourners came and stood with that family. Today's word is the name of the village: Nickel Mines.

Reporters asked how anyone could forgive so fast. The answer the Amish gave pointed back to something old. The Lord's Prayer runs through Amish worship and home life, and in the King James words it says, "And forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." Right after the prayer, Jesus adds: "For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you." Researchers who wrote a book about Nickel Mines, called Amish Grace, heard Amish people describe forgiveness as something decided long before the day it was needed. Prayed into them, over years of ordinary mornings. That's what today's line means. They didn't have to find forgiveness in the worst week of their lives. It had already been chosen, and when the day came, it chose them. Two things it didn't mean. It didn't mean the parents stopped grieving. Forgiving isn't forgetting, and it isn't saying the harm was small. The grief stayed, and had to be walked through. And it didn't mean the matter was simple for everyone else. Christians differ on how forgiveness works. Some point to Jesus in Luke's Gospel, "if he repent, forgive him," and hear forgiveness as waiting on repentance. Others point to Jesus on the cross: "Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do." There, nobody had asked. Both readings are held in good faith. At Nickel Mines, the man could never ask. The forgiveness went to his family anyway, as a visit, a hand, a presence at the grave.

Here's the practice, and go gently with it. Let your breath slow. Think of a family on the other side of some harm: the relatives of someone who hurt others, maybe far away in the news, maybe close to home. Not the harm itself. The family. A mother, a brother, a child carrying a name they didn't choose. If you pray, you can hold them before God. If you don't, simply wish them peace. And if this touches a wound of your own, you don't have to go there today; just rest and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Nickel Mines. A village in Amish country, and the name of a forgiveness that reached the family of the man who did the harm.
Your line: forgiveness chose them. Today, notice one small grudge, and decide now, before it's tested, what you'll do with it. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-four.

howItsDone: Amish Christians pray the Lord's Prayer in worship and at home and speak of forgiveness as a choice made ahead of time; after the Nickel Mines shooting, Amish neighbors visited and comforted the gunman's family.

original.note: Greek: to let go, release, forgive — the verb in the Lord's Prayer's forgive us, as we forgive.
